selectionSummary: One recovery edition for November 5, prepared on November 6 within 48 hours of cutoff. Selected for institutional scale, cross-border consequences and lasting significance: the US congressional transition, reported wartime infrastructure damage, and developing-country financing pressures. This is an editorial selection, not an objective ranking.

snapshot.summary: A coming change in US congressional control raised questions about foreign policy; reports described fresh infrastructure damage in the Russia–Ukraine war; and new debt data highlighted financing pressures across developing economies.
connections: Editorial connection: political oversight, wartime infrastructure vulnerability and borrowing costs can each shape governments' room to act.
uncertainties: Election-driven policy changes, refinery damage and the development effects of new borrowing remained uncertain at cutoff.

stories.title: US election aftermath shifts attention to congressional power and foreign policy
stories.summary: Democrats had won both chambers, with the new Congress due in January. November 5 coverage examined domestic political changes and possible constraints on presidential foreign policy.
stories.whyItMatters: Changes in US spending and oversight could affect allies, military commitments and diplomacy far beyond Washington; electoral victory alone does not establish a policy outcome.
stories.selectionRationale: A major institutional change in a globally influential state, examined through congressional reporting and two distinct international-policy lenses.

stories.title: World Bank report puts developing-country external debt at a record $9.4 trillion
stories.summary: A new World Bank report described a rebound in borrowing alongside increasing financing pressure. Its figures cover 2025, not debt newly incurred on November 5.
stories.whyItMatters: Financing terms influence the resources governments can devote to services and investment. Aggregate debt growth alone does not establish that every borrower faces the same risk.
stories.selectionRationale: A global financing development affecting many economies and their long-term investment capacity, considered through aggregate, national and reform-oriented lenses.
stories.evidenceNote: Anadolu, Nairametrics and The Guardian are independent originating newsrooms. They share the World Bank as an underlying data source, so the common facts concern what its report says, not three independent audits. The Bank's original release was additionally inspected for consistency, not counted as a fourth article. Apparent numerical inconsistencies in ancillary source passages are omitted.
